taxonomy.note: Current Kew accepts Rhus virens and recognizes var. virens and var. australis. The Central Texas evidence used here corresponds to the typical virens concept; the learner remains species-level unless an infraspecific distinction becomes field-useful.

evidence: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Purola Preserve records Rhus virens among naturally occurring species and provides local flower/fruit images.
Travis — UT Plant Resources Center Travis County herbarium index includes Rhus virens var. virens.
Comal — the Harvard University Herbaria isotype specimen of Rhus virens was collected by F. J. Lindheimer at New Braunfels, Comal County, and is currently determined as R. virens subsp./var. virens.
target_zone_range.guardrail: No county inferred from statewide distribution or nursery/horticultural availability. Synonym-based county evidence is counted only where the synonym maps unambiguously to the current taxon concept.

morphology.look_here_first: Look for leathery evergreen foliage: alternate compound leaves usually have only 5–9 thick, smooth-edged leaflets that are glossy dark green above. This immediately separates it from the many-leafleted flameleaf and the 3-leaflet fragrant sumac.
diagnostic_traits: large evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub or small tree
odd-pinnate leaves usually with 5–9 thick leathery leaflets
leaflets entire, glossy dark green above and duller beneath
small creamy-white flowers in compact branched clusters
flattened red drupes covered with red hairs
foliage may bronze/orange after frost but typically persists

confusers.separator: Flameleaf has many narrow leaflets and a strongly winged rachis, then drops leaves after brilliant red fall color; evergreen sumac has fewer, thicker, mostly entire glossy leaflets and retains foliage.
Fragrant sumac has only 3 often lobed/coarsely toothed leaflets and is low/deciduous; evergreen sumac has 5–9 entire leathery leaflets and is a larger evergreen shrub.

diagnostic_roles: glossy upper vs dull lower leaflet
